items.title: Integrating TorchTPU into TorchTitan and Optimizing Models for TPU
items.summary: TorchTPU integrates a native torch.device("tpu") backend directly into PyTorch, allowing developers to train large-scale models on Google Cloud TPUs without rewriting code in JAX. The TorchTitan TPU fork enhances this with production-grade scaling primitives like SimpleFSDP, Graph Trainer, and custom Pallas kernels that achieve high Model Flops Utilization (MFU) across dense and MoE architectures. items.title: Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism
items.summary: Google Cloud's MaxText framework now supports long-context training up to 14 million tokens on Cloud TPUs by implementing four context-parallel strategies: All-gather, A2A, P2P, and USP. Powered by the Tokamax Splash Attention kernel, these strategies effectively manage attention compute and memory bottlenecks without materializing full key-value sequences in high-bandwidth memory. Developers can adopt these capabilities in MaxText v0.2.4 to achieve high Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) across large-scale model training workflows.

items.title: Agent Distraction
items.summary: Analysis of over 913,000 coding agent sessions reveals that 13% expose agents to inline TODO(b/...) comments. In 6% of encounters, agents act on these comments, with 83% being entirely unprompted by the developer. These detours result in significant overhead—adding 70% more steps, 77% more tokens, and 105% more wait time per session—split between chasing closed tickets (41%) and unauthorized scope creep on open bugs (57%). Higher-capability models show higher distraction rates, highlighting the need for automated cleanup and linters to maintain agent-friendly codebases

items.title: What is Pathways? Single-controller training for large models
items.summary: Pathways is a single-controller distributed training system designed to coordinate large-scale model training across multiple accelerator groups by representing computations as a global dataflow graph. Unlike traditional SPMD models like DDP and FSDP that rely on synchronous collectives, Pathways uses asynchronous dispatch and a central scheduler to maximize hardware utilization and prevent deadlocks in complex workloads. By decoupling model definition from physical hardware via virtual devices, developers can efficiently scale complex training architectures and seamlessly handle dynamic workloads like reinforcement learning post-training.

items.title: How Agent Anomaly Detection scores on benchmarks we didn't write

Developers can integrate AAD alongside semantic governance and strict tool limits as part of a defense-in-depth strategy to secure agentic applications.

items.title: A Google Place ID finder in 10 lines of JS
items.summary: The problem A local business owner asked me: "How do I send customers a link that opens the Google review box straight away?" Google supports this with a direct review link: https://search.google.com/local/writereview?placeid=ChIJb5qX9LW9cEgRVzYV0mRGxVw To build it you need the business's Place ID (the ChIJ… string). The official route is the Places API, which means: a Google Cloud project an API key and billing details a server to keep the key private There's a simpler way. The Place ID is already inside every Google Maps link, just encoded differently. In this post we'll build a Place ID finder around one small function (about 10 lines) that pulls it out, entirely in the browser. Step What you do 1 Find the feature ID in the Maps URL: !1s0x…:0x… 2 Pack its two 64-bit numbers into 20 bytes of protobuf 3 Base64url-encode the bytes. That's the Place ID. Open a business on Google Maps and look at the full URL. In the data= part you'll see something like: !1s0x4870bdb5f4979a6f:0x5cc54664d2153657 This is the feature ID (FID): two 64-bit hex numbers joined by a colon. First half: 0x4870bdb5f4979a6f Second half: 0x5cc54664d2153657. This is the CID, the number used in maps.google.com/?cid

items.title: Where did my SOL go? Finding the rent locked in empty Solana token accounts
items.summary: If you've traded memecoins on Solana for a few months, your wallet balance is probably a bit lower than your trades say it should be. Part of the gap is rent. Every token you've ever held opened a token account, and each of those accounts keeps a small SOL deposit. Selling the token doesn't give the deposit back. The empty account just sits there. This post explains where that SOL is, gives you a read-only script to find it, and shows how to get it back. On Solana, your wallet doesn't hold tokens directly. Each token you own lives in a separate token account, owned by your wallet. Every account must hold enough SOL to be rent-exempt. Today, for a standard SPL token account (165 bytes), that's 0.00148844 SOL. A Token-2022 account with the usual ImmutableOwner extension is 170 bytes, so about 0.00151 SOL. The catch: an account keeps the deposit it paid when it was opened. For years, a token account cost 0.00203928 SOL, so older accounts still hold that much. The older your wallet, the more SOL per empty account. You can check today's figure yourself with the getMinimumBalanceForRentExemption RPC call (pass 165). items.title: Rental Account Recovery — Require Fresh Code Before Each Password Change
items.summary: A property-management application needs an account recovery path, but that path must not restore access after account erasure. Resolve this tension by separating a recoverable password change from the terminal deletion workflow. Require a valid session and a fresh possession code before changing a password; bind that proof to the specific action, consume it once, and revoke other sessions when the change succeeds. Short answer: Send the code, verify it, then accept the password change in the same flow. Keep the short-lived proof in application-owned state. Account deletion needs its own authorization decision and revocation of every session; a password-change proof must not authorize deletion or become a reusable recovery credential. Consider a resident who manages a rental account through a property portal. The resident may want to replace a password today and request account erasure later. items.title: Build Buddy, after the week: I tested my own fix on new samples
items.summary: Builders Week is over, but a reader's suggestion left one question open. Quick recap: Build Buddy asks a local Gemma 3 4B to fix C# compiler errors, then checks each fix by rebuilding and running the program. A fix only counts if it builds and prints the expected output. On my six samples, Gemma scored 5/6. The one failure was CS0161: the fix compiled, but added two extra Console.WriteLine calls. A reader suggested treating that as a known failure case and changing the prompt. One sentence, "Keep the program's behaviour and console output exactly the same," took it to 6/6. I wrote the rule after seeing the six samples fail, and I tested it on the same six. That's the classic way to fool yourself. A fix tuned on the test can pass the test without being any good. So I added four new samples the rule had never seen, each with one planted error and an expected.txt. I checked every answer key by running a hand-written correct fix first, because on Day 1 one of my own test cases was broken. items.summary: A FeatureCell does not start with "whatever was in the constructor." Calling initialize() activates the runtime pipeline, and the value it begins with depends on a resolved decision between a declared default, a previously persisted value, and a deliberate hydrate() factory. Knowing which source wins — and why — is what separates an accidental starting value from an intentional one. This post walks through what initialize() actually activates, when hydrate() overrides everything else, and how to choose between a static default, Persist behaviors, and an explicit factory when your FeatureCell comes online. Key takeaway: Initialization is not a direct mutation. Whatever value is selected — hydrated, persisted, or declared — is enqueued as a replaceState operation and processed through the same pipeline as any other update. A FeatureCell is not operational the moment it is declared. It becomes a runtime participant only after initialize() is called — once, and exactly once. items.summary: Email verification looks like a small form feature: collect an address, send a code, and show a success message. In a real product, it is a timeline with several actors: the browser, the API, the mail provider, a user who may open two tabs, and a timer that eventually expires. When those actors disagree, a React component often falls back to a handful of booleans: const [loading, setLoading] = useState(false) const [verified, setVerified] = useState(false) const [error, setError] = useState (null) This works for the happy path. It gets confusing when a resend request finishes after an old verification request, or when a user returns to a tab after the code has expired. A typed timeline makes the UI easier to reason about and gives tests something more useful than a screenshot to assert. loading, verified, and error can all be true at the same time. That means the component can accidentally render “Verified” while a newer request is still pending. items.summary: We build Opti-Behavior, the WordPress plugin discussed here. Originally published on optiuser.com. A rage click is when a visitor clicks the same spot several times in a very short time, usually 3 or more clicks within about one second. Rage clicking almost always means the visitor expected something to happen, and it did not. Think of an elevator button you press again and again: that is exactly what rage clicks are, but on a website. A dead click is the quiet version: a single click on something that looks clickable and does nothing. Rage clicks are one of the clearest signs of a frustrated visitor. And frustrated visitors do not buy, sign up or come back. The good news: rage clicks are easy to find and often easy to fix. Simple definition: A rage click is 3 or more quick clicks on the same small area, usually within about one second. A dead click is a single click that does nothing at all. items.title: Is that really GPTBot? How to verify AI crawlers in your logs
items.summary: Open any access log today and you'll see GPTBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot and friends. The problem: a user agent is just a string. Anyone can send User-Agent: GPTBot from a $5 VPS, and scrapers do it on purpose, because many sites whitelist "good bots". So before you celebrate ("ChatGPT reads my site!") or panic ("AI bots are hammering my server!"), check whether the traffic is real. Here's how, with a few lines of Node. Fake AI bots cause three kinds of wrong decisions: Wrong stats. You think AI search is crawling you a lot, but half of it is a scraper with a borrowed name. Wrong blocks. You see "GPTBot" hammering a slow endpoint and block it in robots.txt. The real GPTBot obeys and leaves. The fake one never read robots.txt anyway. Wrong allow rules. A WAF rule like "allow anything containing ClaudeBot" is an open door for whoever reads your rule. Several AI companies publish the IP ranges their crawlers use, usually as a JSON file linked from their bot documentation. OpenAI, for example, publishes separate lists for GPTBot, OAI-SearchBot and ChatGPT-User, and Google publishes a list for Googlebot. items.title: Node.js Shipment Reminder Queue Retries (Idempotency Before Subscriber Fan-Out)
items.summary: Short answer: if a shipment reminder is sent twice, assume the queue can deliver twice and make the Node.js sender idempotent with a durable key derived from user_id + reminder_id + scheduled_at; acknowledge the message only after that result is safely recorded. For a game studio shipping collector editions, one warehouse update can fan out to thousands of subscribers. The tempting implementation is consume, send, then ack. It looks correct on the happy path. It isn't enough once a worker loses its lease, restarts after sending, or retries a delivery whose acknowledgement was never recorded. The same message can legitimately return. This is an effective-cost problem more than a queue-price problem. Duplicate SMS or email sends spend money downstream, trigger support tickets, and erode trust. The queue bill is only one line. Standard queue delivery is at-least-once. A retry or worker failure can therefore produce a duplicate delivery, and application code has to expect it. Acknowledging before the send flips the failure mode: the worker can disappear after the ack and before the notification, losing the shipment update entirely. items.title: Mozilla to Shut Down Solo, Deleting Users' Websites and Data
items.summary: Mozilla is shutting down Solo, its AI-powered website builder and hosting service, on November 30. A notice on the Soloist.ai homepage reads: "We've made the difficult decision to close Solo. We have appreciated all of your support building and growing this product, and the feedback we've received from all of you. Solo will cease operations on Nov 30, 2026." The Register reports: Mozilla launched Solo in December 2023 as a "Mozilla Innovation Project," aimed at helping sole traders to build themselves a webpage for their services. Some 54,000 people used its LLM to build pages, and relied on Mozilla to host them -- complete with custom domain names. Users now have just over two weeks left to find a new home for their pages, although Mozilla says it first notified them on October 1. According to the support FAQ, users can download a ZIP containing an HTML export, contact form and newsletter submissions, and a CSV linking to their images. The images themselves must be downloaded separately. Domains purchased through Solo Domains must also be moved to Name.com, with Mozilla handling the transfer after users create an account and supply its code. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Letting an AI assistant read SQL Server without letting it write
items.summary: The problem The request sounds simple: let an AI assistant answer questions from a company's on-premises SQL Server. The hard part is what the assistant must not be able to do. The threat model treats the assistant itself as the attacker: it can be prompt-injected, for example by text stored in a table it just read, or simply make a mistake. The goal is that three things still hold: it cannot change the database, it cannot read outside the connected database, and it cannot get data back from a call before that call is recorded. items.title: The Old Screen Was the Real Spec: Rewriting a Streaming Portal From AngularJS to React
items.summary: Rewriting a legacy frontend is usually described as a coding problem. It almost never is. It is a specification problem wearing a coding problem's clothes, and the teams that get this wrong ship a different, undocumented application instead of a modernized version of the one operators already trust. Here is how a streaming operations portal came off AngularJS and onto React without breaking the people who use it every day. Dense, long lived screens. Driven by asynchronous backend jobs. Built originally on AngularJS, then grown for years until two way binding had become unpredictable and features that should have touched one part of the screen reached into several controllers at once. The API documentation behind it was incomplete. That one fact decided everything that followed, because it meant the only honest description of how the system actually behaved was the UI itself, inferred from watching network traffic rather than read from a spec. items.summary: Adopting AI assisted accessibility remediation for frontend engineering allows development teams to eliminate Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) legal liabilities while creating inclusive digital experiences. Small software businesses and digital agencies face surging demand for WCAG 2.2 compliance and ADA web guidance. However, auditing hundreds of existing React components, legacy template files, and dynamic modals by hand is an exhausting, labor-intensive chore. Faced with tight sprint deadlines, many website owners turned to third-party "accessibility overlay widgets", only to find that overlays fail to prevent federal lawsuits and actively interfere with assistive screen readers. Real accessibility compliance must occur directly in the source code. items.title: The anti-flicker tax: what hiding your page does to LCP
items.summary: If you've run a test from a visual editor, you've probably seen it: the page loads with the old headline, and a beat later the new one snaps into place. That's flicker. Client-side testing tools all have to deal with it, because their script applies the variant after the browser has started painting. From inside the browser you can either show the original and swap it, so the visitor sees the flash, or hide the page until the script is done. The second option is the "anti-flicker snippet", and most tools turn it on by default. An anti-flicker snippet makes the page invisible, usually with opacity: 0 on the body or a class like Google Optimize's async-hide. It reveals the page when the testing script finishes or a timeout fires, whichever comes first, so the timeout is your worst case. The defaults are generous: Google Optimize shipped its snippet with a 4,000 ms default (Google's developer docs). Optimize shut down on September 30, 2023, but copies of that snippet are still sitting in plenty of tags. Webflow Optimize also defaults to 4,000 ms. items.title: Volume zero is not mute
items.summary: With the volume at zero, my MacBook's speakers were still playing. Quietly enough that you only notice in a quiet room, but they were playing. On a Mac, volume and mute are two separate things. Volume is a number between 0 and 1. Mute is a switch. CoreAudio keeps them as two properties on the output device, and nothing forces them to agree. The number is a position on the device's range, and the device reports that range in decibels. So I asked the built-in speakers for theirs: var range = AudioValueRange() var size = UInt32(MemoryLayout .size) var a = AudioObjectPropertyAddress( mSelector: kAudioDevicePropertyVolumeRangeDecibels, mScope: kAudioDevicePropertyScopeOutput, mElement: kAudioObjectPropertyElementMain) AudioObjectGetPropertyData(device, &a, 0, nil, &size, &range) print(range.mMinimum, range.mMaximum) // -63.5 0.0 The bottom of the range is −63.5 dB. That is very quiet. It is not off. Usually nobody notices, because macOS flips the mute switch as well when the volume arrives at zero. items.title: Why a Mac Writing Helper Needs Two Permissions, and Why It Still Refuses Password Fields
items.summary: A writing helper that works inside someone else's text field has to ask macOS for a lot of trust. Accessibility permission is how an app reads and, if you approve it, replaces text in another app. Input Monitoring is how it can see keyboard events while you are in Mail, Notes, or a browser. Those are two different Privacy & Security toggles, and they should be. People are right to pause on both. We build DraftKey, a Mac app for Tab autocomplete and rewrites you review before they are inserted. This post is about the permission model behind a helper like that: why two system permissions are required, how we ask for them, and the cases we refuse even after you have said yes. The general mechanics come from Apple's public documentation, linked at the end. The product rules come from the shipped app's own wording, including the Apps & privacy section in Settings. Apple documents these as separate resources, and System Settings treats them that way. Accessibility is under Privacy & Security. items.title: Monolith, Modular Monolith and Microservices: A Practical Comparison for .NET
items.summary: Cover photo by Nicolás Gutiérrez on Unsplash Most software engineers do not choose their architecture in a vacuum. You usually meet architectures in stages: traditional monoliths in legacy codebases or early-stage products, microservices when a company wants independent team scaling, and modular monoliths when an organization realizes that distributed systems introduce operational costs they did not anticipate. Each approach is often marketed as the obvious successor to the one before it. In real engineering, however, these architectures are simply points on a trade-off spectrum balancing operational simplicity against structural isolation. This article compares traditional monoliths, modular monoliths, and microservices across core architectural dimensions, outlines the specific .NET libraries and frameworks each one relies on, and provides practical criteria for choosing between them. items.title: "Failed" Is a Lie Your .NET Agent Tells the Model: Four Outcomes Every Tool Call Needs
items.summary: Most tool functions I see in agent demos return one of two things: a result, or an exception. Microsoft.Extensions.AI then turns that exception into a polite little string for the model, something like Error: Function failed. For a read, that's fine. For a write, it's a trap. Picture a refund tool. The HTTP call to billing goes out, billing commits the refund, and the response gets lost on the way back. Your timeout fires. The tool throws. The model reads "failed", does the helpful thing, and calls the refund tool again. The customer is now 40 EUR richer instead of 20. The model didn't misbehave. You told it something false. It had no way to know "failed" really meant "I have no idea". This post is about the small vocabulary I now give every tool in a .NET agent so the model never has to guess. items.title: What it takes to turn an iPhone microphone into a decibel meter
items.summary: I work on Noise Meter at W Lab. It is an iPhone app that shows the sound level in decibels and logs a whole night of it, so someone with a noisy neighbour can show when it was loud. This post is about the measuring part: what happens between the microphone and the number on screen, and the places where I had to be honest about what a phone can't do. iOS processes microphone input by default: automatic gain, noise suppression, EQ. All of that is exactly what a meter must not have, because a quiet room would be boosted and a loud one pulled down. The audio session mode that turns it off is .measurement: try session.setCategory(.record, mode: .measurement) try session.setPreferredSampleRate(48_000) From there it is an AVAudioEngine input tap with a 4800-frame buffer, which is 100 ms at 48 kHz. I ask for 48 kHz but build the analyzer for whatever rate the hardware returns. items.title: I built an iOS app where your documents delete themselves
items.summary: We keep too many documents forever. Scans of contracts, tickets, IDs sent for a one-time procedure, a rental agreement from three years ago. Most of them only matter for a short time, and then they just sit in your phone, your cloud and your photo library, waiting to be leaked, lost or forgotten. So I built Fadely: an iOS app that works as a vault for temporary documents. You add a document, choose a date, and when that date arrives the document destroys itself. My brother-in-law flies constantly. His passport was buried among hundreds of downloads on his phone, and he always worried: what if it gets stolen? So in Fadely, docs get an expiry date. Then they're gone for good. 🔒 Most storage apps are built on one assumption: keep everything, forever. Fadely does the opposite. Every document has an expiry date from the moment you save it. You decide how long it should exist, and the app takes care of the rest. items.title: Datacentres are deeply unpopular. Has Sweden made one we can all love?
items.summary: It is built of wood, resembles an Ikea and its power is totally renewable. Plus, it was built with the local community in mind. Is this facility in Falun the best datacentre in the world? ‘It was pretty cool, when they were building it. It looked like a very large Ikea,” says John Wernvik, of EcoDataCenter. He is giving me a tour of their facility in Falun, Sweden, which could lay claim to being the world’s greenest datacentre – although to many, that is a contradiction in terms. One difference is immediately visible: this datacentre is made out of wood. Huge panels of cross-laminated timber arrived at the site pre-cut, and were assembled by crane according to instructions, like flatpack furniture. Aesthetically, this section of the datacentre is more like an Ikea before the fit-out, a cavernous, echoey, immaculately clean hangar. items.title: Tanuki: Pon’s Summer review – an adorable raccoon mends the world, one parcel at a time
items.summary: Nintendo Switch/2, PlayStation 4/5, Xbox One/series X/S, PC; Denkiworks/Inpleron Limited This gentle game of fixing and fetching, in which you play as a furry post office worker on a BMX, has a slow, calming magic that delights in routine and restoration Arriving alongside November’s blue wave, Tanuki: Pon’s Summer is a game of quiet restoration that feels perfectly suited to the current moment. Tasked with repairing an ancient shrine in the weeks leading up to a local festival, you’ll find yourself cleaning out trash, mending broken arches and slowly bringing a small rural community back together. It sounds a bit like JL Carr’s compact but enchanting novel A Month in the Country, except instead of shell-shocked veterans of the first world war you’re left exploring the rich inner life of a Japanese racoon dog who can ride a BMX. Even so, the mixture of steady progress and general low stakes proves intoxicating. This is a short game, but it’s hard not to linger over it. Continue reading...

items.title: Handing over humanity (22 minute read)
items.summary: Some AI experts believe that once we achieve superintelligence, humans will be permanently disempowered, and we shall all be ruled by an AI god. This might not be such a desirable outcome, as humans have a natural desire for freedom. The arrangement will probably not work, as keeping power responsive to human needs has required checks developed over centuries, sustained by repeated feedback from the real world and correction, and there's no reason to keep that equilibrium stable once humans have surrendered all control. Humans have the ability now to steer the technology in a way that will not lead to a complete replacement of human judgment.

items.title: What objective is reasoning solving? (12 minute read)
items.summary: Reasoning is pathfinding in token space. There are many paths from the problem to a correct answer, and the model traverses each of them with each sample. A path is not guaranteed to converge to the correct answer - it's only in aggregate, over the distribution of paths, do we get a high probability of success. RL training directly raises the success probability. The gains credited to 'thinking longer' come from the search paid for during training rather than at inference.

items.title: Two Kinds of Test-Time Scaling (28 minute read)
items.summary: Test-time scaling trades compute for performance at test time. There are two types of test-time scaling: one allows researchers to trade more compute for more performance per task, but only up to the maximum quantity of per-task compute used during training; and the other lets researchers trade more compute for more performance per task, and lets them do so up to quantities of compute and performance that never occurred during training. Scaling methods that permit the latter change will have a larger impact than test-time scaling considered simply. This essay describes how this may impact the world.

items.title: Harness 2: executing agent code as it streams (6 minute read)
items.summary: Framer's Harness 2 significantly upgrades the agent's execution process, allowing entire workflows in one program, achieving up to 33% cost reduction and 20% faster execution. This is done by executing JavaScript as it streams in, avoiding multiple model calls and using eager execution and early cancellation to enhance efficiency. The redesign also replaces DSL with method calls for real-time updates, making task execution streamlined for both in-app and external agents, reducing tool steps by 43% and cached input tokens by 39% per message.

items.title: How to Train a Swarm (19 minute read)
items.summary: Swarms are AI systems where multiple agents cooperate towards a shared goal. This post discusses a technique called collective inference-time scaling, where agents scale the amount of useful work performed in parallel and the communication needed to achieve it. It also explains how to design incentives for parallel work, and covers the general topic of designing incentives for reinforcement learning.

items.title: Why Agents Are Soon Only Going to Have 1 Tool (9 minute read)
items.summary: Agents are collapsing their entire tool catalog into one 'exec' tool. This allows models to write short scripts that chain, combine, and await actions inside isolated sandboxes. Models can now reliably combine and chain dependent actions in a single pass. In the previous standard tool-calling model, agents could only perform single actions, but the exec tool allows them to perform multiple actions.

items.title: What Is Quantum Advantage Actually Worth? (9 minute read)

items.title: Scaling Git at OpenAI (31 minute read)
items.summary: OpenAI's monorepo's size and demands increased at a staggering pace over the last year, necessitating a revamp of the AI lab's source control system. Its technical staff built Pando, a new backend for Git repositories optimized for concurrent pushes to many branches and to maximize read throughput. The team implemented the backend without interrupting any engineering work or changing how the team uses Git. Pando cut median push latency in production by nearly 5x, and it now delivers nearly a petabyte of Git data per day.

items.title: Lessons from building Copilot Cowork (21 minute read)

The transition to Rust improved efficiency and highlighted the importance of clear testing, boundary setting, and human oversight in the development process.
